13720:
To resent something or someone means to feel a lasting, bitter anger toward them because you believe they treated you unfairly, disrespectfully, or in a way you didn't deserve.

It's not just being annoyed. It's not just being upset in the moment. Resentment is the feeling that sits inside you — sometimes for days, months, or even years — because a wound hasn't healed.
What makes it different from ordinary anger

Regular anger can flare up and fade quickly. You stub your toe, you feel pain and frustration, and then it's gone. Resentment doesn't work that way.

When you resent someone, you hold onto the negative feeling. It smolders quietly. Every time you see that person, or every time something reminds you of what they did, that bitter feeling comes back. It's anger with memory.

Think of it this way: anger is a fire; resentment is the ash that stays warm long after the fire is out.

The key ingredient is a sense of injustice. You resent something when you feel:

  • You were treated unfairly
  • You were disrespected or humiliated
  • You were overlooked or not given what you deserved
  • Someone took advantage of you
  • You were forced to do something against your will
  • You were blamed for something that wasn't your fault

The feeling says: "This wasn't right. I didn't deserve this."

Importantly, you don't have to be objectively right for resentment to form. What matters is that you perceive the situation as unfair. Resentment is about how you feel, not necessarily about what actually happened.

• A student studies hard all semester but fails the exam while a classmate who barely studied passes. The student resents the teacher for what feels like unfair grading.
  • A woman has been working at a company for five years. A newcomer gets promoted over her without explanation. She resents her manager for the decision.
  • A child is always compared to their more successful sibling by their parents. As an adult, they still resent their parents for the way they were raised.
  • A man sacrifices his personal goals to support his family financially, but his family never acknowledges his efforts. He begins to resent them for taking him for granted.
  • A friend constantly cancels plans at the last minute. After many times, you resent them for not valuing your time.
What you can resent — the objects of resentment

Grammatically and in real life, you can resent:

A person:
"She resents her older brother."

An action or decision:
"He resents the fact that he was passed over for the promotion."

A situation or condition:
"They resent being treated like children at work."

Something someone said:
"She resented his comment about her appearance."

An experience:
"He resents every moment he spent in that toxic job."

Notice that you can even resent abstract things — a rule, a system, a circumstance — as long as you feel it wronged you in some way.
Grammar: how "resent" works in a sentence

The most important grammar pattern to know is that "resent" is very commonly followed by a gerund (a verb ending in -ing), not an infinitive.

✅ "I resent being ignored."
❌ "I resent to be ignored." ← This is wrong in English.

This is because "resent" refers to an experience that already happened or is ongoing — something you feel about an action — and gerunds are used for that in English.

Other patterns:

  • resent + noun/pronoun: "He resented her." / "She resented the decision."
  • resent + gerund: "I resent being treated unfairly."
  • resent + that-clause: "He resented that no one thanked him."
  • resent + possessive + gerund: "She resented his constant interrupting."

Resentment sits at a moderate-to-deep level of emotional intensity. It is:

  • Stronger than simple annoyance or irritation
  • Quieter and more internal than explosive rage
  • More specific than general dislike — it's tied to a particular wrong done to you
  • More personal than indifference — there's a wound underneath it

It's also worth noting that resentment often grows in relationships where there is some closeness or expectation. You tend to resent people who mattered to you, or whose opinion of you mattered. We rarely deeply resent strangers. We resent parents, friends, colleagues, bosses — people whose actions had real weight in our lives.
How to tell if someone "resents" rather than just "dislikes"

If someone simply dislikes a person, they just don't enjoy their company. But if someone resents a person, there's a story behind it — a specific thing that happened, a specific way they felt wronged. Resentment always has a reason, even if that reason is never spoken aloud.

A person might resent their father and still love him. A person might resent a close friend and still want their friendship. This is what makes resentment complex — it can exist alongside other emotions, and it doesn't necessarily mean you hate someone. It means a wound hasn't closed.
A one-line summary to anchor it all
To resent = to feel a lasting, bitter anger toward someone or something because you believe they treated you unfairly or in a way you didn't deserve.
13721:
If someone is resentful, they carry a deep, lasting feeling of bitterness and anger inside them because they believe they were treated unfairly, wronged, or disrespected — and they haven't been able to let go of it.

It is not just ordinary anger. It is anger that stays. It simmers quietly inside a person, sometimes for days, months, or even years.
Breaking It Down Simply

Imagine this: Your colleague at work takes credit for a project you worked hard on. Your boss praises your colleague in front of everyone, and you get nothing. You feel it is deeply unfair.

Now, two things can happen:

  1. You feel angry in that moment, speak up, and then move on.
  2. You feel angry — and that anger doesn't leave. Every time you see your colleague, it comes back. You feel bitter. You feel unappreciated. You feel like you were cheated. You can't forget it.

The second case is resentment. And the person feeling this is resentful.
The Three Key Ingredients

For someone to be resentful, three things are almost always present:

1. A wrong (real or imagined)
Something happened that the person felt was unfair, hurtful, or disrespectful — whether it truly was or not. This is important: a person can be resentful even over a misunderstanding, as long as they believe they were wronged.

2. A feeling of "I didn't deserve this"
Resentful people feel their suffering was unearned or unjust. There is a strong sense of: "I did nothing wrong. Why did this happen to me?"

3. The feeling doesn't go away
This is what separates being resentful from just being angry. Resentful feelings linger. They build up over time. The person replays the event in their mind. The wound stays fresh.
How a Resentful Person Feels Inside

Being resentful is an uncomfortable emotional state. The person may feel:

  • Bitter — a sour, unpleasant feeling toward the person who wronged them
  • Unappreciated or overlooked — like their efforts, feelings, or worth were ignored
  • Powerless — like they couldn't stop the unfair treatment
  • Unfairly treated — a constant, nagging sense of "This isn't right"
  • Unable to move on — the past event keeps pulling them back emotionally
How It Shows in Behaviour

A resentful person doesn't always express their feelings directly. The bitterness often leaks out in subtle ways:

  • Giving the silent treatment to someone they resent
  • Being uncooperative or unhelpful toward that person
  • Making sarcastic or cold remarks
  • Avoiding the person who wronged them
  • Holding grudges — refusing to forgive even long after the event
  • Acting passive-aggressively (being difficult without openly admitting why)
How "Resentful" Differs from Similar Words

This is important for a learner, because several words seem similar but are different.

Resentful vs. Angry
Anger is often immediate, hot, and short-lived — you flare up and then cool down. Being resentful is slower, colder, and much longer-lasting. You can be angry for five minutes. You can be resentful for five years. Resentfulness is essentially anger that has been stored and not released.

Resentful vs. Jealous
Jealousy is the fear of losing something you already have — like being jealous of someone who seems to be getting closer to your best friend. Resentful is about feeling wronged by someone's actions toward you, not about fear of losing something.

Resentful vs. Envious
Envy is wanting something someone else has — their success, their looks, their money. Resentfulness is bitterness over how you were treated, not about what someone else has. However, in real life, the two can overlap: you might resent someone and envy them at the same time.

Resentful vs. Bitter
These are very close in meaning. "Bitter" describes a broader, more generalised sour feeling — sometimes toward life itself or toward the world. "Resentful" is more specific: it is almost always directed at a particular person or situation that caused you pain. Someone who has been let down repeatedly for many years might become bitter; someone who was passed over for a promotion last month might be resentful.
The Target of Resentment

Resentfulness is almost always directed at someone or something specific:

  • Resentful of someone (the person who wronged you): "She is resentful of her stepmother."
  • Resentful toward someone: "He grew increasingly resentful toward his employer."
  • Resentful about something (the unfair situation): "They felt resentful about the way the decision was made."
  • Resentful for something (what was done): "She was resentful for being excluded from the meeting."
Degrees of Being Resentful

Like most emotions, resentfulness exists on a scale:

  • Mildly resentful — a small, quiet irritation that hasn't grown yet
  • Resentful — a clear, persistent bitterness that affects how you feel about a person
  • Deeply resentful — a strong, consuming bitterness that significantly colours your thoughts and behaviour
  • Consumed by resentment — the feeling has taken over, making it very hard to think about anything else
Real-Life Sentences

Here are examples to show how the word is used naturally:

  • "He was resentful of his younger sister because she always seemed to get whatever she wanted."
  • "After being overlooked for promotion three times, she grew deeply resentful toward her manager."
  • "The workers were resentful about the pay cuts while the executives got bonuses."
  • "You could see from his resentful expression that he hadn't forgiven her yet."
  • "Growing up in his sibling's shadow left him resentful for years."
  • "She tried not to feel resentful, but the unfairness of it kept coming back to her."
An Important Nuance: Real vs. Perceived Injustice

Resentfulness does not require that you were actually wronged. What matters is that you believe you were wronged.

For example: A parent may treat both children equally, but one child might still feel they received less love. That child can be genuinely resentful, even if the parent did nothing wrong. The feeling is real, even if the injustice isn't.

This is why resentment can sometimes be difficult to resolve — the other person may not even understand why you are resentful, because from their perspective, nothing unfair happened.
Why It Matters to Understand This Word

Resentfulness is one of the most common and powerful emotional states in human relationships. It quietly damages friendships, families, and workplaces. It is at the heart of many conflicts that people cannot explain clearly. When you understand what it means, you will start noticing it everywhere — in books, in news, in conversations, and perhaps even in yourself.
One-Line Summary
Resentful means feeling a deep, lasting bitterness and anger toward someone because you believe they treated you unfairly — and you haven't let go of that feeling.
13722:
Resentment is a deep, lasting feeling of bitterness and quiet anger that you carry inside yourself toward a person, group, or situation — because you believe they treated you unfairly, wronged you, or disrespected you in some way.

The key word here is believe. Resentment doesn't require that the wrong actually happened. What matters is that you feel it did. You feel you deserved better, and you didn't get it.
What Makes It Different from Regular Anger

This is important, because resentment is often confused with simple anger.

Anger is immediate and loud. You stub your toe — you feel angry right now, intensely, and then it fades.

Resentment is slow and silent. It doesn't explode. It simmers. It stays with you for days, months, or even years. It lives quietly in the background of your mind, and it can flare up whenever you think about — or even see — the person or situation that caused it.

Think of anger as a fire that burns bright and dies out. Resentment is like hot ash underneath — it looks calm on the surface, but the heat never really goes away.
What Resentment Feels Like on the Inside

When you feel resentment, you tend to:

  • Replay the past. Your mind keeps going back to the moment you felt wronged. You re-live it, re-examine it, and re-feel the hurt.
  • Think "it's not fair." There is a strong sense of injustice. You feel you were cheated, overlooked, taken for granted, or treated worse than you deserved.
  • Feel a kind of cold hostility toward the person who wronged you — not necessarily explosive anger, but a quiet bitterness. You may not want to talk to them, help them, or be around them.
  • Feel powerless. Often, resentment grows when you couldn't do anything about the wrong at the time — maybe you couldn't speak up, couldn't leave the situation, or the other person simply didn't care.

Resentment typically grows from situations like these:

  • You worked very hard, but someone else got the credit.
  • A person made a promise to you and repeatedly broke it.
  • You were always the one giving in a relationship, and the other person never gave back.
  • Someone humiliated or disrespected you, especially in front of others.
  • You were treated unfairly compared to someone else — a sibling who was favored, a colleague who was promoted over you.
  • You were forced into a situation against your will and had to stay silent about it.

Notice that all of these situations have something in common: you felt you deserved better, and you didn't receive it. And importantly, you likely had no power to fix it at the time.

Resentment isn't always directed at others. You can also feel resentment toward yourself — a bitter feeling that you let yourself down, that you made the wrong choices, or that you allowed others to treat you badly when you should have stood up for yourself.
How Resentment Is Different from Similar Words

Grudge: A grudge is what you hold — a decision to stay angry at someone. Resentment is what you feel — the emotional experience itself. The two go together: if you hold a grudge, you likely feel resentment.

Envy: Envy is wanting something another person has (their success, their beauty, their possessions). Resentment is feeling wronged by another person. You can feel envy without feeling resentment, and vice versa. However, they can mix — for example, resenting a colleague for getting a promotion you think you deserved more.

Bitterness: Bitterness is what resentment becomes when it has been left unresolved for a very long time. If resentment is a wound that won't heal, bitterness is the scar that changes you. A bitter person has let old resentments shape their entire outlook — they become permanently cynical, distrusting, or negative.

Indignation: Indignation is a sharper, more righteous flash of anger at unfairness — like witnessing an injustice and immediately feeling outraged. It's usually short-lived. Resentment is deeper and much more personal; it's about your own experience of being wronged, and it lingers.
How Resentment Affects People and Relationships

Resentment is quietly destructive — to both you and your relationships.

  • It poisons relationships gradually. You may start distancing yourself from the person, becoming cold, sarcastic, or uncooperative — sometimes without even realizing why.
  • It affects your behavior without obvious cause. You might snap at someone, refuse to help them, or undermine them — driven by old resentment that you never addressed.
  • It drains you mentally and emotionally. Carrying resentment is exhausting. It occupies mental space and can contribute to stress, anxiety, and even depression.
  • It traps you in the past. Because resentment revolves around replaying old wrongs, it keeps your emotional energy anchored to something that is already over.

There is a well-known idea that holding onto resentment is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to get sick. The person you resent may have moved on completely — while you are still carrying the weight of what they did.

• After years of being ignored by her manager, she couldn't hide her resentment anymore.
  • He smiled and said everything was fine, but she could sense the resentment underneath his words.
  • Growing up, he harbored deep resentment toward his parents for the opportunities they never gave him.
  • She didn't feel resentment — she had long since made peace with what happened.
  • The resentment between the two brothers had been building for decades, rooted in a single decision their father made.
If you had to remember just one thing: Resentment is a lingering, bitter feeling of anger toward someone you believe treated you unjustly — a wound that keeps hurting because you haven't let it go.
13723:
At the heart of every meaning of reservation is one simple idea: setting something aside, or holding something back — keeping it separate from everything else.

Whether you're talking about a table at a restaurant, a doubt in your mind, or a stretch of land, something is being kept, held, or withheld for a specific purpose or reason.
Meaning 1: A Booking or Arrangement (Most Common)

When you contact a hotel, restaurant, airline, or any service and ask them to keep something for you at a future time, you are making a reservation. The reservation is the arrangement itself — the confirmed promise that something will be held for you.

"I'd like to make a reservation for two at 7 PM."
"Do you have a reservation under the name Singh?"
"I lost my reservation confirmation email."

What's being "set aside" here is a physical spot, a seat, a room, or a ticket — kept specifically for you, not given to anyone else until you arrive.

Key detail: A reservation is made in advance — before you actually use the thing. You reserve it now so it's waiting for you later. Once you've actually used the service (you've eaten the meal, checked out of the hotel), the word "reservation" no longer applies to that transaction.

Common collocations:

  • make a reservation
  • hold a reservation
  • cancel a reservation
  • confirm a reservation
  • reservation number / reservation code
  • hotel/restaurant/flight reservation
Meaning 2: A Doubt, Hesitation, or Concern

When you are not fully comfortable agreeing with something — when some part of your mind says "wait, but..." — you have a reservation.

"I support the plan, but I have reservations about the timeline."
"She accepted the offer without reservation." (meaning: without any doubt at all, completely)
"He had serious reservations about trusting her."

Here, "reservation" means something you are withholding — specifically, your full, unconditional agreement. Part of your consent is being held back.

Notice that this meaning almost always appears in the plural ("reservations") when you're expressing doubt. The singular "reservation" is more common in phrases like "without reservation" (meaning completely, wholeheartedly).

Nuance: A reservation is gentler than a flat-out objection. If you have a reservation, you're not saying "no." You're saying "yes, but..." — you're leaning toward agreement while something still nags at you.

Common collocations:

  • have reservations (about something)
  • without reservation
  • express reservations
  • deep/serious reservations
  • voice/share one's reservations
Meaning 3: A Piece of Land Set Aside for a Specific Group or Purpose

In certain formal or official contexts, a reservation is an area of land that has been officially designated — separated from surrounding land — for a particular group of people or a specific use.

The most prominent use: In the United States and Canada, a reservation (also called a "reserve" in Canada) is land that the government has formally set aside for Indigenous/Native peoples to live on and govern. These are sovereign territories with their own laws and governance.

"The Navajo Reservation is the largest Native American reservation in the United States."
"He grew up on a reservation in South Dakota."

More broadly, land can also be "reserved" for nature and wildlife:

"a wildlife reservation" / "a nature reservation"

(though the word reserve is often preferred in these cases — "a nature reserve" — "reservation" is less common here but still used)

The idea is the same: land is set aside, separated from general use, and dedicated to something specific.
Meaning 4: A Condition, Qualification, or Exception

In formal writing and speech, a reservation can also refer to a specific limitation or exception attached to an agreement or statement — a condition you're keeping in mind even while broadly agreeing.

"The committee approved the proposal with certain reservations."
"I accept your argument, but with one reservation: the data is from 2015."

This is closely related to Meaning 2 (a doubt), but with a slightly more formal tone. Here, the reservation is almost like a written footnote — you're agreeing, but you're specifically carving out an exception or noting a limit to your agreement.

All four meanings come from the same underlying logic:

MeaningWhat is being "set aside" or "held back"?
BookingA physical spot, room, or seat
DoubtYour full, unconditional agreement
LandA geographical area
QualificationYour complete, exception-free acceptance

Actually, let me put that in plain words instead:

In a booking, a place or spot is set aside for you. In a doubt, your full agreement is being held back. On designated land, a territory is set apart. With a qualification, your complete acceptance is withheld. Every single time, something is being kept separate, held in reserve, not fully given over.
Common Phrases and Patterns Worth Knowing

"Without reservation" — completely, with no hesitation, no doubts whatsoever.

"I recommend her without reservation." (= I have zero doubts about recommending her.)

"Have reservations about" — to feel uncertain or uneasy about something.

"I have reservations about quitting my job so suddenly."

"Under reservation" — sometimes used to mean something is being held pending a confirmed booking (less common in everyday speech, more formal/legal).

"Make a reservation" — to book something in advance.

"Can you make a reservation at that new Italian place?"

• It is not the same as cancellation (that's when a reservation is ended or withdrawn).
  • It is not the same as a guarantee — a reservation can sometimes still be cancelled by either party.
  • It is not the same as a refusal — having reservations means hesitating, not outright saying no.
  • It is not the same as a preference — a reservation is a formal or official act of setting something aside, not just wanting something.

Reservation is a noun built around the idea of holding something apart — keeping it back from the general flow. In daily life, it most often means a booking (a table, a room, a seat held for you in advance). In your thoughts and feelings, it means a doubt or hesitation — the part of you that hasn't fully agreed yet. In geography and governance, it refers to land officially set aside for a specific community or purpose. And in formal language, it can mean a qualification or exception you're attaching to your agreement. The same word fits all four meanings because they all share the same core: something is reserved — separated, held, and not just given away freely.
13724:
To reserve means to hold something back or set it aside deliberately — keeping it separate from general use, so it's available for a specific purpose, person, or moment.

Think of it this way: imagine you have something valuable — a seat, a portion of food, your energy, your opinion. Instead of giving it away freely or using it right now, you consciously hold it back and direct it toward something specific. That act of holding back with intention is what "reserve" captures.

This one core idea — deliberate holding back — runs through every use of this word. The context changes what is being held back and why, but the essence stays the same.

1. To arrange for something to be kept for your use — booking, securing in advance

This is probably the most everyday use. When you reserve something, you claim it ahead of time so it won't be given to anyone else.

"I reserved a table at the restaurant for 8 o'clock."
"She reserved two seats at the front of the auditorium."
"He reserved a room at the hotel a month before his trip."

You haven't used the thing yet — but you've ensured it will be there when you need it. The seat is being held back from other customers, specifically for you.

Notice the effect: by reserving, you create a kind of guarantee. The thing is no longer available to the general public — it's been pulled aside and labelled with your name, so to speak.

2. To keep or set aside something for a particular purpose or person

Here, you're not necessarily booking it in advance from someone else — you're physically or mentally separating a portion of something and directing it toward a specific use.

"Reserve a cup of the pasta water before you drain it — you'll need it for the sauce."
"The front rows are reserved for the families of the performers."
"Set aside a little of your budget and reserve it for unexpected expenses."

The key here is purpose. You're not just saving something randomly — you have a reason in mind. You pull it out of the general pool and dedicate it.

This sense is used very naturally in cooking, planning, and resource management.

3. To save something for a more important moment or use

This is closely related to meaning #2, but the emphasis shifts slightly — here, you're saving something for a later or more special occasion, often because using it now would be wasteful or premature.

"Reserve your energy for the final kilometres of the race."
"She reserved her finest crockery for special guests."
"Don't use all the spices at once — reserve some for the final stage of cooking."

The idea is about timing and priority. You could use it now, but you deliberately choose not to, because there's a more important use coming up.

4. To retain a right, authority, or power — keeping it in your own hands

When a person or organisation reserves a right, they are saying: "This authority or power belongs to us and we are not giving it up or transferring it to anyone else."

"The management reserves the right to refuse entry."
"I reserve the right to change my mind."
"All rights reserved." (This phrase on books and creative works means: the creator is keeping all legal rights — no one else can copy or reproduce this without permission.)

This use appears often in legal, formal, and contractual language. The "right" is being held back from others — it stays with the person who stated it.

5. To hold back a judgment, opinion, or decision — deliberately not expressing it yet

Sometimes what is being reserved is not a physical thing but something internal — a thought, a verdict, or a reaction. When you reserve your judgment or opinion, you choose not to express it yet. You hold it back until you have more information, or until the right moment.

"The judge reserved her verdict until she had reviewed all the documents."
"Let's reserve our judgment on the new employee until we've seen her work for a few weeks."
"He reserved his comments for the end of the meeting."

This is a sophisticated and important use. It signals intellectual caution and discipline — you're not rushing to speak or decide. You're keeping your conclusion held back, in a kind of internal reserve, until you're ready.

Whether you're reserving a hotel room, reserving pasta water, reserving the right to edit a contract, or reserving your judgment on someone — the same thing is happening:

Something is being deliberately held back, pulled out of the general flow, and directed toward a specific use or moment.

What changes across the senses is simply what is being held back:

  • A physical space or object (a seat, a room, a portion of food)
  • Energy or resources
  • A right or authority
  • An opinion, judgment, or emotional reaction

Reserve vs. Save
"Save" is a broader, more casual word — you can save a file, save someone's life, save money. "Reserve" carries a more deliberate, controlled, often formal flavour. When you reserve something, there's always a sense of purpose — you know what it's being held back for. "Save" doesn't always carry that specificity.

Reserve vs. Book
"Book" is specifically about making formal arrangements with an external party — you book a flight, a hotel, a table. "Reserve" is wider: it covers booking (you can reserve a table), but also covers non-booking uses like reserving your energy, reserving a right, or reserving judgment. You would never say "I booked my judgment" — but you can "reserve" it.

You'll frequently encounter this word in the passive: something is reserved for something/someone.

"These seats are reserved for ticket holders."
"This line is reserved for senior citizens and people with disabilities."
"That expression of emotion is reserved for private moments."

This just means someone has already carried out the act of reserving — the thing has been set aside and is now dedicated to that purpose.

The verb reserve is a word of deliberate restraint and directed intention. Whenever you see or use it, ask yourself: What is being held back? For what purpose or for whom? Answer those two questions and the meaning will always be clear.
13725: A reservoir is a place where a large amount of something — most often a liquid — is collected, held, and stored so that it can be used when needed. Think of it as a "savings account," but instead of money, it stores things like water, oil, or even ideas. The defining quality of a reservoir is that it acts as a supply that you draw from over time — it is not just a passing flow, but a stored body that stays put.

When most people say "reservoir," they mean a large body of stored water, usually meant to supply a city, town, or farming region.

Reservoirs of this kind come in two forms:

1. Man-made (artificial) reservoirs — These are the most common type. Humans build a dam across a river, which blocks the natural flow of water. As the water has nowhere to go, it backs up and collects, forming a huge lake behind the dam. That lake is the reservoir. Cities then pipe water from it for people to drink, cook with, and bathe in. A good example is the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, which created Lake Mead — one of the largest reservoirs in the world.

2. Natural reservoirs — Sometimes, a natural lake or even a large underground layer of rock acts as a reservoir. The water simply gathered there over thousands of years on its own, and humans tap into it.

The key point is the purpose: a reservoir is not just any lake. It is water that is being managed and stored for a specific use.

A reservoir does not have to sit on the surface. Deep underground, porous rock (rock full of tiny holes, like a sponge) can be soaked with water, oil, or natural gas. These underground pockets of stored liquid or gas are also called reservoirs. When an oil company drills a well, they are drilling down to reach an oil reservoir — a layer of rock that has been holding oil for millions of years.

In the same way, underground water reservoirs (called aquifers) supply wells across the world. Many farms and rural homes depend entirely on water pumped up from these hidden reservoirs.

The word is also used for small containers inside machines or devices that store a liquid needed for the machine to work.

For example:

  • A car has a brake fluid reservoir — a small plastic tank under the hood that stores the fluid needed to make the brakes work.
  • A fountain pen has an ink reservoir — the chamber inside the pen that holds the ink.
  • A car's windshield wiper system has a washer fluid reservoir.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: a dedicated holding space that stores a liquid so it is ready to be used as needed.

Because a reservoir suggests a large, deep, available supply, people also use the word figuratively — meaning they apply it to things that are not physical liquids at all.

You might hear or read sentences like:

  • "She has a deep reservoir of patience." — She has a great deal of patience stored within her, ready to be drawn on.
  • "The country has a vast reservoir of talent." — There are many talented people available in that country.
  • "His years of experience gave him a reservoir of knowledge." — He has accumulated so much knowledge that he can draw from it like water from a well.

In all these cases, the speaker is painting a picture: just as a water reservoir is a large, dependable store you can draw from, this person or place has a large, dependable store of something valuable.

In science, especially in medicine and biology, reservoir has a very specific meaning. It refers to a species, animal, or environment that permanently carries and harbors a disease-causing germ (like a virus or bacteria) without being seriously harmed by it itself.

For example, bats are considered a natural reservoir for certain viruses. The virus lives inside the bat population across generations. The bats generally do not get sick from it, but the virus can sometimes jump from bats to humans, causing outbreaks. In this sense, the bat population is the "storage place" for the virus — it is where the germ lives and waits, just like water waits in a dam.
What Ties All These Meanings Together

No matter which context you see the word "reservoir" in, three ideas are always present:

  1. Storage — Something is being held and kept, not just passing through.
  2. Quantity — There is a significant amount of whatever is being stored.
  3. Future use — The stored thing is being kept precisely because it will be needed and drawn from later.

If you remember these three ideas — stored, substantial, and available for use — you will understand the word "reservoir" correctly in any sentence you ever encounter it.
13726:
To reside somewhere means to live there as your home — in a settled, established way. It is not about visiting a place or passing through. It means that place is where you actually belong, sleep, and have made your life.

"She resides in Tokyo."

This means Tokyo is her home. She lives there. It is where her life is based.

"Reside" and "live" mean almost the same thing, but there is an important difference in tone and formality.

  • "Live" is the everyday, casual word. You use it in normal conversation.
  • "Reside" is the formal version. You see it in official documents, legal papers, news articles, and formal writing.

Think of it this way: you would say "Where do you live?" to a friend at a coffee shop. But a government form would ask "State the city where you currently reside."

Both sentences ask for the same information. The word "reside" just sounds more serious, official, and polished.

This is a critical distinction. "Reside" always implies permanence or long-term settlement. It is not temporary.

  • If you are at a hotel for three days → you are staying there, not residing.
  • If you are visiting your parents for a week → you are visiting, not residing.
  • If you moved to a city and that is now your home → you reside there.

The idea of roots, stability, and an established home is baked into the meaning of "reside." A person who resides somewhere has made it their base of life — not just a temporary stop.

Here is where "reside" becomes even more interesting. The word is also used beyond physical places. It can describe where a quality, a power, a feeling, or an idea "lives" — meaning where it exists or is found.

"True power resides in the people, not in the government."

This does not mean people literally live inside something. It means power belongs to, is located in, or is held by the people. The power has its "home" there.

More examples of this figurative use:

"The real problem resides in the way the system was designed."

→ The problem is found within the design itself.

"Wisdom does not reside in age alone."

→ Wisdom is not simply located in or guaranteed by old age.

"The final decision resides with the manager."

→ The authority to decide belongs to, and sits with, the manager.

In all these cases, think of "reside" as asking: "Where does this thing have its home? Where does it belong or exist?" — and then answering that question.

Reside is always followed by a preposition. The most common ones are:

  • reside in → used with cities, countries, buildings, or abstract things
    "He resides in Canada." / "The issue resides in the code."*
  • reside at → used with a specific address
    "She resides at 14 Elm Street."*
  • reside with → used when authority, power, or a right belongs to someone
    "The final say resides with the committee."*

Since you want to fully understand this word, knowing its family will help you recognize it in different forms:

  • Resident (noun) → a person who resides somewhere
    "She is a resident of New York."*
  • Residence (noun) → the place where someone resides; the act of residing
    "His residence is in the countryside." / "She took up residence in Rome."*
  • Residential (adjective) → relating to where people reside
    "This is a quiet, residential neighborhood."*
  • Residing (present participle) → the ongoing action
    "The family residing in that house has lived there for decades."*

13727: Residence means the place where a person lives, or the fact/state of living in a particular place. It is a formal, slightly official-sounding word. When you think of "residence," think of it as the more serious, grown-up version of words like "home" or "house."
The Two Main Layers of Meaning

This one word carries two related but distinct ideas. Understanding both is key.

1. A Place Where Someone Lives

This is the most common use. Here, "residence" refers to the physical building or location a person calls home — particularly on a long-term or permanent basis.

"The doctor's residence was a quiet apartment near the hospital."
"Please write your current residence on the form."
"The ambassador's residence was a grand old building in the city."

Notice that it doesn't just mean any building — it means the place where someone actually lives. A hotel room you stay in for two nights is not your residence. The flat where you sleep every night, keep your belongings, and return to after work — that is your residence.

2. The Act or State of Living Somewhere

Here, "residence" refers not to the building itself, but to the fact that someone lives (or lived) in a particular place, and often for how long.

"After ten years of residence in Canada, he applied for citizenship."
"Her residence in that village lasted only two summers."
"The law requires five years of continuous residence before you qualify."

In this sense, you are not talking about a building — you are talking about the condition, the period, the status of being a resident of a place.

"Residence" is frequently used in formal, legal, and official settings. This is because it carries a sense of permanence and legitimacy that casual words like "home" do not.

On government forms and legal documents:
"Place of residence" is the official phrase used to ask where you permanently live.

"State your place of residence: _"

For important or official homes:
Leaders, dignitaries, and heads of state often have an official residence — a home that comes with their position, not just a private house they own.

"10 Downing Street is the official residence of the British Prime Minister."
"Rashtrapati Bhavan is the official residence of the President of India."

When someone is described as being "in residence" at a place (especially a university, institution, or organization), it means they are officially stationed there for a period of time — living and working there as part of a formal arrangement.

"She was appointed as the writer in residence at the university for one year."
"The sculptor is currently in residence at the arts centre."
"The doctor completed his training while in residence at the hospital."

This phrase signals an official, recognized presence — not just a casual visit.

Understanding a word fully also means knowing how it differs from words that seem similar.

Residence vs. House
A house is just the physical structure — the walls, roof, and rooms. A residence is a house (or flat, or any dwelling) considered as the place someone lives in. Every residence is a building of some kind, but not every building is a residence.

Residence vs. Home
Home is warm and emotional — it suggests belonging, comfort, family, memory. Residence is neutral and formal — it describes where you live as a fact, not a feeling. You would say "home" to your friends; you would write "residence" on a legal document.

Residence vs. Address
Your address is simply the string of information (street number, city, pin code) that locates you on a map. Your residence is the actual place where you live. Your address tells people where to find your residence. The two are closely linked, but they are not the same thing.

Residence vs. Accommodation
Accommodation just means a place provided for someone to stay — it could be temporary (a hotel, a hostel). Residence implies something more settled and permanent.

One of the most important things to understand about "residence" is that it carries a strong sense of permanence or at least long-term staying. It is not about short visits.

If you spend a weekend in another city, that hotel is not your residence. If you live in a city for years, working, paying bills, building a life — that city is your place of residence.

This is why "residence" matters so much in legal and official contexts: governments, banks, and institutions want to know where you truly, stably live — not where you are passing through.

Here are the most important phrases you will encounter with this word:

PhraseMeaning
  • Place of residence — where you officially live; used on forms
  • Primary/permanent residence — the main place where you live long-term, as opposed to a holiday home
  • Official residence — a home tied to an official position or role
  • Country of residence — the country you currently live in
  • Take up residence — to begin living in a new place
  • In residence — officially stationed at and living/working at a place
  • Legal residence — where you are officially registered as living, for legal purposes
  • Proof of residence — a document (like a utility bill or bank statement) that proves you live at an address

Residence, as a noun, means:

  1. The place where a person lives, especially permanently or long-term — a formal, official way to refer to someone's home.
  2. The state or period of living in a place — the fact that someone resides somewhere, and for how long.

It is a word associated with formality, officialdom, and permanence. You will encounter it on forms, in legal documents, in news about heads of state, and in descriptions of academic or artistic appointments. It is never a casual or emotional word — it is precise, neutral, and serious.
13728:
Residency means the condition or state of living in a particular place. When you are a resident somewhere — meaning you actually live there, not just visit — that act or status of living there is called your residency.

But this single word has grown to carry several distinct and important meanings depending on the context. Each meaning is connected to this core idea of "being stationed somewhere for a period of time," but they play out very differently in real life.
Meaning 1: The General Sense — Living Somewhere

In its most ordinary use, residency simply refers to the fact of living in a place, especially on a long-term or official basis.

"Her residency in Mumbai spans over twenty years."

Here, it just means the ongoing condition of making a place your home. It is not about visiting or passing through — it implies a settled, stable presence.
Meaning 2: Legal Residency — The Right to Live in a Country

This is one of the most commonly encountered uses, especially in legal, immigration, and governmental contexts.

Legal residency refers to the officially recognised status that allows a person to live in a country or region where they are not a citizen. Governments issue this status (often called a "residency permit" or "permanent residency") to foreigners who meet certain conditions — such as having a job, family ties, or fulfilling an investment requirement.

This is different from citizenship. A person with residency has the legal right to live and often work in a country, but they may not have the full rights of a citizen — such as voting. "Permanent residency" (sometimes called "PR") means this right has no expiry date, though it usually comes with conditions too. "Temporary residency" means the right is granted only for a fixed period.

"She applied for permanent residency in Canada after living there on a work visa for three years."

The key idea here: residency is a legal status granted by an authority that permits someone to be in a place as an official inhabitant.
Meaning 3: Medical Residency — The Training Period for Doctors

This is a specialised but extremely widespread use of the word, particularly in countries like the United States, India, and many others.

After a person earns their medical degree (becoming a doctor in the basic sense), they are not yet fully qualified to practise independently. They must spend a period — typically anywhere from three to seven or more years — working under supervision at a hospital, gaining hands-on clinical experience in their chosen specialisation. This period of supervised, immersive, practical training is called a residency.

The doctor in this phase is called a resident. They work long hours, treat real patients, make real decisions — but always under the oversight of senior doctors. The word "residency" here comes from the old tradition of doctors literally residing (living) at the hospital during their training, though today residents do not always live on-site.

"After finishing her MBBS, she matched into a residency programme in cardiology at a teaching hospital in Delhi."

The key idea here: a residency is a structured, official period of professional training embedded within an institution, where the trainee both learns and works at the same time.
Meaning 4: Artist or Academic Residency — A Creative or Scholarly Placement

In the world of arts, literature, music, and academia, a residency refers to a period during which a creative person or scholar is formally hosted by an institution — such as a university, arts centre, gallery, or cultural organisation — to pursue a project, create work, or engage with the community there.

The institution typically provides the person with a workspace, funding, housing, or some combination of these. In exchange, the artist or academic may give lectures, hold workshops, exhibit work, or simply create during their time there.

"The novelist was awarded a six-month residency at a writers' retreat in the mountains, where she completed her second book."

"The university offered him a residency as a poet-in-residence, where he would run workshops for students."

The key idea here: a residency is a temporary but immersive period of focused work, made possible by an institution that invests in you and your work.
Meaning 5: Performance Residency — Repeated Shows at One Venue

This use is very common in the music and entertainment world. When a musician, band, DJ, or performer is booked to perform multiple times at the same venue — rather than a single one-off show — that ongoing engagement is called a residency.

"The jazz band held a weekly residency at a popular club in Bangalore every Friday night."

"The pop star announced a six-week residency at the O2 Arena in London."

This meaning comes from the same root idea: instead of touring from city to city, the performer stays (resides) at one place for a sustained period. It has become a prestigious model in the music industry — artists like Adele and Celine Dion have done famous residencies in Las Vegas, for example.
Meaning 6: Official Residence — A Building or Place of Stay

Less commonly, "residency" can also refer to a physical building or compound that serves as an official or formal home — especially in a historical or diplomatic context.

"The Governor's residency was a large colonial building at the edge of the city."

In this sense, it is close to saying "the official residence" — the place where someone of authority or importance formally lives.

Notice how all these uses share the same underlying thread: being in one place, in an established and purposeful way, for a meaningful period of time.

Whether it is a migrant earning the legal right to stay in a country, a young doctor planted in a hospital to learn their craft, a novelist nestled in a mountain retreat to write, or a band taking up regular nights at a jazz club — in each case, someone is residing somewhere with intention and structure. That is what "residency" captures.

• General: The condition or state of living somewhere — "twenty years of residency in this city."
  • Legal/Immigration: An official status granting the right to live in a country — "permanent residency," "residency permit."
  • Medical: A post-degree training period for doctors inside a hospital — "surgical residency," "she is in her second year of residency."
  • Arts/Academia: A formal period of creative or scholarly work hosted by an institution — "artist residency," "writer-in-residence."
  • Performance/Music: A recurring engagement at a single venue — "the band has a residency at that club every weekend."
  • Physical place: The official home or building of an authority — "the governor's residency."
13729:
A resident is a person who lives in a particular place — not just passing through, not on a short visit, but actually based there in an ongoing, settled way.

The key idea locked inside this word is permanence (or at least, long-term presence). A resident has planted their life, however partially, in a specific location.

When people say someone is a resident of a place, they mean that place is where that person calls home — where they sleep, where they receive mail, where their daily life happens.

"She is a resident of Mumbai."
"The residents of this building complained about the noise."
"Long-time residents of the village remember when this road didn't exist."

Notice that "resident" can refer to someone living in a country, a city, a neighborhood, an apartment building, or even a specific institution like a care home or hostel. The word scales across all these levels.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where precision really matters. Several words seem similar but mean different things:

  • A visitor or tourist is in a place temporarily — a few days or weeks. They are not residents.
  • A guest is invited and temporary by nature.
  • A citizen is a legal member of a country (by birth or naturalization). A citizen has rights tied to belonging. A resident, on the other hand, simply lives there — without necessarily having those full legal rights of citizenship.
  • A tenant is someone who rents a property. They can also be a resident, but "tenant" emphasizes the rental relationship, while "resident" emphasizes the act of living there.

You can be a resident without being a citizen — this is very common. For example, someone from India living and working in Canada with a visa is a resident of Canada but not a Canadian citizen. They live there, but they haven't been granted full legal membership in that country.
The Legal Sense: "Legal Resident" or "Permanent Resident"

In formal, legal, or immigration contexts, "resident" takes on a more precise meaning.

A legal resident (or permanent resident) is someone who has been officially granted the right to live in a country by its government — even though they are not a citizen of that country. Many countries have a formal status for this.

"She applied to become a permanent resident of the United States."
"He holds permanent resident status in Australia."

This is distinct from someone who is living in a country without official permission, or on a temporary visa. Those people are physically residing there, but they may not hold the official status of "legal resident."

So in everyday speech, any person who lives in a place can be called a resident. But in legal speech, a "resident" (especially with words like "legal," "permanent," or "lawful" in front) refers to someone who has government-approved status to live there long-term.

This is a completely separate but very common meaning, especially in healthcare.

In medicine, a resident (also called a resident doctor or simply a resident) is a doctor who has graduated from medical school but is still in a period of supervised, hands-on training inside a hospital or clinic. They are qualified doctors — they've earned their degree — but they are not yet independent specialists. They are learning under the guidance of more experienced doctors.

"The resident examined the patient before the senior doctor arrived."
"She worked 80-hour weeks as a first-year resident."
"He's doing his residency in cardiology." (Here, "residency" is the noun form of the training period itself.)

The connection to the original meaning is historical — in the past, these trainee doctors literally lived (resided) in the hospital. That practice has faded, but the name stuck.

A resident doctor sits between a medical student (who is still studying) and a fully independent consultant or specialist (who has completed all training). They have real responsibility for patients but are still supervised and learning.

In places like care homes, nursing homes, rehabilitation centers, boarding schools, or hostels, the people who live there are called residents.

"The residents of the nursing home gathered in the common room."
"Each resident has their own room."

This usage simply emphasizes that these people live in the institution as their primary home, often long-term. It's a respectful, neutral term — preferred over words that might suggest they are merely patients or inmates.

Resident as a noun always points to one thing: a person who lives in a place with some degree of continuity and settlement. The exact shade of meaning shifts depending on context:

  • In everyday use: someone who lives in a city, town, building, or neighborhood.
  • In legal/immigration use: someone officially permitted to live in a country long-term without being a citizen.
  • In medicine: a qualified doctor in a structured training program at a hospital.
  • In institutional use: someone who lives in a care home, school, or similar facility.

What ties all these uses together is the same underlying idea — this person belongs to this place, at least for now, in a way that a passerby or visitor simply does not.
